description: A one-person team from Warsaw, led by a conservator-restorer of contemporary art.
summary: Left Behind is an interactive notebook for school-age space enthusiasts. A small robot wakes up on the Moon with one mission: document what people left behind and decide how to protect it. It visits four places: Tranquility Base, the Surveyor 3 probe, the Apollo 17 rover and a laser mirror from Apollo 15. At each one the player learns who made the object and why, looks at its condition, and chooses what should happen to it next. Afterwards the robot tells them what actually happened. I am a conservator, so I built the decisions on the way conservators think about contemporary art. The game uses NASA photographs and a NASA map from 1972, together with my own drawings in pencil on tracing paper. It also includes narration, voice answers, larger text and high contrast for players with low vision, and runs offline from a single file. And after the last act, a short surprise ending asks what to do with the strangest objects left on the Moon.
details:
What it is

Left Behind is a browser game for children aged about 8 to 14. Since the 1960s, astronauts and robots have left hundreds of objects on the Moon. Most children have never thought of them as heritage. In the game, a small robot wakes up on the Moon with one mission: document what people left behind and decide how to protect it. The player makes those decisions with it.

How it works

Each act follows the same rhythm. First the player reads the object’s story: who built it, why, and what went wrong or right. Then they scan the object. They lift sheets of tracing paper to uncover a real NASA photograph, and for the rover a hand-drawn map of damage, and click details to look closer. The robot always separates what it can see in photographs and records from what it can only suppose, such as damage from dust, solar radiation or cold. Some clues add a new piece of context to the notebook, and a few conservation options only unlock once the player has found the right context. After that the player chooses what matters most about the object and what to do with it: protect it where it is, repair it, take it to a museum, keep it in an archive, or let time do its work. If a choice goes against the value they picked, the robot says so. Each act ends with what actually happened and a report card that fills in by itself. At the end the player can download the robot as a small page that keeps the colours of their decisions.

The story

The game is a tragedy in five acts, with the robot as the chorus. The acts are Tranquility Base (Apollo 11), Surveyor 3, the Apollo 17 rover and the Apollo 15 laser reflector. In the last act the robot’s battery runs low and it realises that it will also become an object left on the Moon. The player decides what should happen to it. At the end the robot asks the question from the beginning again: why protect things that nobody can see? A short satyr play about the 96 bags of astronaut waste follows the credits. The game is written as the robot’s notebook, because conservators document before they decide, and the record often outlives the object. The tragedy gives the notebook its shape and its stakes: in the end the robot finds that it is becoming an object left behind, and its notebook may be all that remains.

Why a conservator

I am a conservator-restorer of contemporary art. NASA has published recommendations for protecting the Apollo sites (2011), but there are no methods yet for conserving objects in space, so the decisions in the game are an experiment. They are inspired by how conservators think about contemporary art and time-based media: valuing a work, caring for installations, accepting change, and strategies such as storage, migration, emulation and reinterpretation.

Look and sound

NASA photographs and a NASA map from 1972 stand for facts. My pencil drawings on tracing paper stand for memory and interpretation. The robot’s status panel is inspired by the Apollo guidance computer display, and its voice uses radio static and the Quindar beeps heard in Apollo transmissions.

Accessibility

The game can read every page and every list of choices aloud, with a choice of voice and tone. Players can answer by voice with a number, a letter, “next” or “back”. Tapping the page replays the last few seconds, and a double tap reads it again from the start. There are also larger text and high contrast modes. Everything spoken is also shown as text. These options are meant for children with low vision or limited hearing, but I have not tested them with those players yet.

Tools

One HTML file with CSS and JavaScript, hosted on Netlify. Narration and voice answers use the browser’s Web Speech API. Fonts and images are embedded, so the game also works offline, except voice answers in some browsers. A chapter menu in Settings lets you jump straight to any act.

How AI was used

Claude, an AI assistant, helped me write the code and edit the English texts. It also processed my hand drawings: removing the paper background, aligning them to NASA photographs, cutting them into parts for animation and combining parts of the same drawing. It wrote the code for the animations and the tracing paper effects, and placed the site markers on the NASA map from official coordinates. It did not generate any drawings or photographs. The only lines it added are the typed labels and pointer lines on the rover outline, the 75 metre circle on the map, the dotted outlines of the missing camera and scoop, and a few short joins where the antenna was erased from the robot drawing, and the misty texture of the tracing paper is partly generated in code. The concept, the story, the conservation logic and all drawings are mine, and the facts were checked against the sources listed below. The demo video was also put together with Claude: it recorded the game footage automatically, cut and cropped my phone clips, and added the English subtitles and sound effects. The hand-drawn tracing shots in the video are filmed by me.

Who it is for

Teachers and museums can use it to introduce space history, space science and the idea of heritage in one lesson.
